title: Debugging Practice Exam
description: Practice reading tracebacks, using pdb, and measuring performance with cProfile and timeit.

questions.prompt: What is a good first debugging step when code fails?
options: Read the error message and traceback carefully
questions.explanation: The traceback points to the failing line and exception type.

questions.prompt: What does print() debugging mean?
options: Inserting print statements to inspect variable values
questions.explanation: Temporary prints reveal what the program is doing at runtime.

questions.prompt: A debugger lets you pause execution and inspect variables line by line.
questions.explanation: pdb and IDE debuggers help step through code beyond print statements.

questions.prompt: help(some_function) shows:
options: The function's source file on disk only
questions.explanation: help() and dir() explore what an object can do.

questions.prompt: import pdb; pdb.set_trace() is used to:
options: Start an interactive debugger at that line
questions.explanation: set_trace drops into pdb when that line runs.

questions.prompt: In pdb, the n command typically:
options: Steps to the next line in the current function
questions.explanation: n (next) executes the current line and stops at the next.

questions.prompt: The bottom line of a traceback usually shows:
questions.explanation: TypeError, ValueError, etc. tell you what went wrong.

questions.prompt: Reading traceback frames from bottom to top shows where the error was raised.
questions.explanation: The last frame is the immediate cause; frames above show the call chain.

questions.prompt: cProfile is used to:
options: Measure where a program spends time
questions.explanation: Profiling finds slow functions in real runs.

questions.prompt: timeit.timeit() helps you:
questions.explanation: timeit runs code many times to compare approaches fairly.

questions.prompt: Before optimizing, you should usually:
options: Profile to find the actual bottleneck
questions.explanation: Measure first; optimize what actually costs time.

questions.prompt: A NameError often means a variable was used before it was defined.
questions.explanation: Check spelling and that assignment happened before use.

questions.prompt: dir(obj) without arguments in pdb or a shell shows:
questions.explanation: dir lists attributes and methods to explore APIs.

questions.prompt: Reproducing a bug reliably means:
options: You can trigger it again with known steps
questions.explanation: Reproduction is required before you can verify a fix.

questions.prompt: Logging compared to random prints:
options: Levels and format can be controlled in one place
questions.explanation: logging is structured; prints are fine for quick checks.

questions.prompt: Rubber duck debugging means explaining the problem out loud to clarify your thinking.
questions.explanation: Teaching the code line by line often reveals the mistake.

questions.prompt: After fixing a bug, you should:
options: Re-run the program and add a test if possible
questions.explanation: Verify the fix and prevent the bug from returning.

questions.prompt: python -m pdb script.py runs:
options: script.py under the debugger from the start
questions.explanation: The -m pdb flag starts pdb before the first line runs.

questions.prompt: An off-by-one error often appears as:
options: IndexError or wrong loop count by one
questions.explanation: Check range bounds and whether you used < vs <=.

questions.prompt: Smaller test cases help isolate which input triggers a failure.
questions.explanation: Shrink the example until the bug is obvious.
